c.tagline: Where the Tigris meets 1,400 years of history.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; fares are agreed with the driver upfront or set by common route, and shared 'service' taxis charge a fixed per-seat price.

emergency.medical: 122 (ambulance service is limited/unreliable; private hospitals or embassy contacts are often faster)
emergency.note: National emergency hotline 112; fire 115. Foreign visitors should also keep their embassy's emergency line on hand.

avoid.reason: Most governments advise against non-essential travel; in particular avoid Sadr City, protest gatherings, and movement outside secure areas after dark.
Use vetted drivers rather than street taxis, steer clear of demonstrations, checkpoints, and military convoys, and keep a low profile at all times.

hood_desc: Baghdad's buzzing commercial and dining hub on a bend of the Tigris, packed with markets, cafes and mid-range hotels; a walkable, comparatively relaxed base for first-time visitors.

Home to the fortified International (Green) Zone with government buildings, embassies and the city's most secure five-star hotels; suited to diplomats, journalists and business travelers who prioritize security.
An upscale, leafy shopping and residential district with malls, embassies and modern restaurants; popular with expatriates, NGO staff and diaspora Iraqis visiting family.
A quieter university peninsula wrapped by the Tigris, home to the University of Baghdad and tree-lined streets; a calmer choice for academics and longer-stay visitors.
The historic east-bank core around Rashid Street and Mutanabbi Street, dense with old markets, bookshops and budget hotels; best for culture-focused travelers wanting old-city atmosphere.
lodging: Al Harithiya House for Hotel Apartments

water.note: Infrastructure and contamination issues make tap water unsuitable for drinking; use bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver; there is no rechargeable transit card. Shared 'service' taxis running fixed routes are far more common than public buses and are paid per seat in dinars.
transit.hours: Public buses and shared taxis generally run roughly 6am-10pm; after that, private taxis or ride-hailing apps are the only options.
transit.note: Public transit is minimal and unreliable; most residents and visitors rely on private cars, shared service taxis, or ride-hailing apps. A metro system is under construction with completion targeted around 2029.

train: Iraqi Republic Railways (limited domestic services to Basra, Mosul and Fallujah from Baghdad Central Station)
bus: Intercity buses/shared taxis from Baghdad's Nahda and Alawi garages to Basra, Erbil, Najaf and Karbala

airport.name: Baghdad International Airport (BGW)
airport.drive: 25-40 min depending on traffic and security checkpoints

transit.m: No public bus/metro serves the airport

tip.r: Not traditionally required, but rounding up taxi fares and leaving 5-10% at upscale restaurants and hotels is appreciated.

food.name: Masgouf
food.desc: Iraq's national dish: river carp butterflied, brushed with tamarind and turmeric and cooked upright beside an open fire, then finished over embers.

places.name: Abu Nuwas Street riverside grills
places.note: The traditional masgouf strip along the Tigris; fish picked live from tanks.

places.name: Khan Baghdad Restaurant
places.note: Well-known city restaurant serving masgouf and grills in a heritage-style setting.

places.name: Dawa Restaurant
places.note: Popular with locals and visitors for masgouf at fair prices with warm service.

food.name: Quzi
food.desc: Slow-roasted lamb served on spiced rice with almonds, raisins and sometimes a thin bread base; the dish brought out for weddings and feasts.

places.name: Khan Baghdad Restaurant
places.note: Large platters of quzi over biryani-style rice, good for sharing groups.

places.name: Karrada restaurants
places.note: The city's busiest eating district, with several kitchens doing whole-lamb quzi.

places.name: Al-Mansour restaurants
places.note: Upmarket western district where formal Iraqi dining rooms serve feast dishes.

food.name: Kubba
food.desc: Shells of bulgur, rice or potato stuffed with spiced minced lamb and onion, then fried or dropped into a sour stew; every region has its version.

places.name: Shorja Market food stalls
places.note: Baghdad's oldest market, where snack counters fry kubba through the morning.

places.name: Karrada restaurants
places.note: Home-style Iraqi kitchens here list several kubba types on one menu.

places.name: Al-Rashid Street eateries
places.note: Old-city street with long-standing counters for kubba and other everyday plates.

food.name: Dolma
food.desc: Vine leaves, onions, peppers and courgettes packed with spiced rice and lamb, layered in a pot and cooked in tamarind or pomegranate until sour-sweet.

places.name: Karrada restaurants
places.note: Family kitchens along the district serve dolma as a lunchtime home-cooking dish.

places.name: Khan Baghdad Restaurant
places.note: Traditional Iraqi menu that usually includes dolma among the cooked dishes.

places.name: Al-Mansour restaurants
places.note: Comfortable dining rooms serving the slow-cooked dishes rather than just grills.

food.name: Samoon with geymar
food.desc: Diamond-shaped bread pulled hot from a stone oven and eaten at breakfast with geymar clotted cream and date syrup, or split for kebabs later.

places.name: Shorja Market bakeries
places.note: Stone ovens fire samoon from dawn beside the spice and date stalls.

places.name: Al-Mutanabbi Street cafes
places.note: Book-street breakfast spots serve samoon with geymar, honey and tea.

places.name: Karrada bakeries
places.note: Neighbourhood bakeries sell samoon by the bagful all through the day.

food.name: Kebab and tikka
food.desc: Minced lamb kebab and cubed tikka grilled over charcoal, served with grilled tomato, raw onion, sumac and hot samoon or khubz bread.

places.name: Karrada grill houses
places.note: Charcoal grills line the main street and stay busy well past midnight.

places.name: Al-Mansour restaurants
places.note: Smarter kebab houses in the west of the city, popular for family dinners.

places.name: Abu Nuwas Street
places.note: Riverside places grill kebabs alongside the masgouf if you do not want fish.

food.name: Chai
food.desc: Strong black tea brewed dark, sweetened heavily and served in a small waisted istikan glass; the backbone of Baghdad social life.

places.name: Shabandar Cafe
places.note: Historic book-street tea house, a Friday institution for writers and readers.

places.name: Al-Zahawi Cafe
places.note: Century-old cafe named for the poet, still pouring tea in the old quarter.

places.name: Beiruti Cafe
places.note: Riverside tea garden on the Tigris, good for tea and shisha after dinner.

food.name: Jallab and sherbet
food.desc: Chilled non-alcoholic coolers: jallab of date and grape molasses with rose water, pine nuts and raisins, plus fruit sherbets and salted laban.

places.name: Shorja Market juice stalls
places.note: Date-syrup and molasses sellers mix jallab to order in the old market.

places.name: Karrada juice bars
places.note: Rows of juice counters serving sherbet, laban and fresh pomegranate juice.

places.name: Abu Nuwas Street stands
places.note: Riverside kiosks sell cold drinks and laban to families walking the corniche.

landmarks: Al-Kadhimiya Shrine (Kadhimiya Mosque)
A breathtaking golden-domed Shia shrine complex with gleaming minarets, one of the most visited pilgrimage sites and architectural showpieces in Iraq.
Abu Hanifa Mosque
A revered Sunni mosque in the Adhamiyah district honoring the founder of the Hanafi school of jurisprudence, known for its striking minaret and dome.
National Museum of Iraq
Home to one of the world's greatest collections of Mesopotamian antiquities, including treasures from Ur and Babylon spanning thousands of years of civilization.
Al-Mustansiriya Madrasah
Founded in 1227, this is one of the oldest surviving universities in the world, its elegant courtyard and brickwork reflecting Baghdad's golden age of learning.
Al-Mutanabbi Street
Baghdad's historic bookselling street lined with booksellers and cafes, named for a celebrated 10th-century poet and beloved as the intellectual soul of the city.
Baghdad Tower
A soaring telecommunications tower with a revolving restaurant offering sweeping panoramic views, standing as a modern symbol of the city's skyline.
Al-Shaheed Monument
A striking split turquoise dome memorial honoring Iraqi soldiers who died in the Iran-Iraq War, its dramatic modernist design visible across the city.
Al-Zawraa Park
Baghdad's largest public park and zoo, offering shaded gardens, a lake, and green space that provide residents and visitors a peaceful escape from the city.
Umm al-Qura Mosque
Also called the Mother of All Battles Mosque, this vast complex features minarets shaped like Scud missiles and a Quran said to be written in Saddam Hussein's blood.
Al-Faw Palace
A grandiose former presidential palace built on an artificial lake, its massive domes and marble halls reflecting Baghdad's era of monumental architecture.

dom.op: Iraqi Republic Railways (IRR) — tickets at Baghdad Central station, no online booking

train.note: There are no international trains from Iraq. Domestically, IRR runs one nightly overnight sleeper between Baghdad Central and Basra (departs ~19:00, arrives ~06:00). IRR has no working booking website and no online sales — tickets are bought at the station on the day of travel.

intl.op: private Iraqi transport companies and GMC shared vehicles — tickets at the terminal, no online booking
private Iraqi transport companies — tickets at the terminal, no online booking

bus.note: International coaches/GMC shared vehicles run from Baghdad toward Amman (Jordan) across the desert highway, and to Iran (Mashhad/Qom for pilgrims), operated by private Iraqi transport companies with no single official booking site. Check security and border conditions before travelling.

ferry.note: Baghdad is inland and has no passenger ferries. Iraq's only significant port, Umm Qasr near Basra, handles cargo rather than scheduled passenger sailings.

half.name: Karbala
half.blurb: Sacred Iraqi city famed as a major Shia pilgrimage destination and religious center.

half.name: Al Ḩillah
half.blurb: Euphrates River city known for its agriculture and proximity to ancient Babylon.

half.name: Ramadi
half.blurb: Riverside city on the Euphrates, historic capital of Iraq's Anbar province.

half.name: Al Fallūjah
half.blurb: City on the Euphrates west of Baghdad, historically known as a bridge town and trade center.

half.name: Sāmarrā’
half.blurb: Ancient city on the Tigris famed for its spiral minaret and Islamic heritage.

full.name: As Sulaymānīyah
full.blurb: Cultural hub of Iraqi Kurdistan, ringed by mountains and known for its lively bazaars.

full.name: Kirkuk
full.blurb: Ancient multi-ethnic city in northern Iraq known for its oil industry and citadel.

full.name: Najaf
full.blurb: Sacred Iraqi city known as a major center of Shia Islamic pilgrimage and learning.

full.name: Ad Dīwānīyah
full.blurb: Agricultural city on the Euphrates in southern Iraq known for its date palms and farming.
